title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Seating Plans
author: Joel, Geeks Who Teach
summary: In 2027, James, Head of History at Elysium Academy, sat in front of a camera. He was going through a curriculum that he has taught hundreds of times acting as if he had a group of students in front of him. Asking questions, counting down for pupils to show their mini-whiteboards, and giving expert explanations on effects feudal lords had upon their subjects. It was a good few weeks of work. This was a UK Government project, funded by Google, to train their AI on what good classroom instruction looks like. James was paid for this and Elysium Learning Trust was keen to take part as they are a 'Forward Thinking' organisation, always striving to keep up to date with the latest research and EduTech hoping to crack the nut on how best to implement AI into the classroom. The project was deemed a success. Due to James signing up to take part in the project, his likeness was used to create a package that schools could purchase to use when teachers were absent, or staffing meant that there would be no subject specialist teaching students. James was just one of a few teachers who had their likeness used to teach the National Curriculum. For the first time ever, every subject was offered to schools. Even Classics! BBC News - AI has entered the classroom - but is it the solution for overworked teachers? An expert teacher, curated through AI and synced with the schools MIS system, knows every pupil's personal details and needs, SEND or otherwise, to guide the asking of questions to individual students. Even their seating plans were algorithmically chosen to limit distractions. The price was relatively cheap, far cheaper than the rates offered by supply agencies so schools jumped on board. Obviously, behaviour does still needed to be managed so a teaching assistant was assigned to the lesson to remove or discipline students for not following the instructions of AI James. Google, looking at their own data were proud to say that more than 50% of schools in the UK were onboard and were using their AI Supply system. So they expanded. ClassAI is a suite, offered by Google, that not only provided a suite of AI deepfake teachers to deliver expert content, but also comes with 30 AI powered tablets that replaced the student's antiquated mini-whiteboards. When the teacher asks a question they answer on their tablet, if they get it right, it automatically adds praise points. If they get it wrong, the tablet offers some advice on where they went wrong along with some questions to check their understanding. A truly ground-breaking personalised education. Computer Weekly - Six companies selected as AI tutoring development partners Google, and their team of marketing executives, targeted their advertising at schools like Elysium Academy. Large amounts of disadvantaged students, high staff turnover, and results either below or well below average. These schools saw small improvements. The lessons were predictable and the routines expected of pupils became second nature. They were to watch a screen, answer the questions and, if they did not follow the expectations of ClassAI, the TA would be escorting them to another room to regulate themselves before returning. UK's first AI classroom without teachers sparks debate The DfE wanted to see some of this in action. They commissioned Ofsted to conduct a review into the use of ClassAI and similar programmes offered by Microsoft, SpaceX, and OpenAI to see their implementation and effectiveness. What they did report on, however, is that many schools weren't just using them to cover lessons for staff absences, or to plug gaps in recruitment challenges, they were being used as the primary method of teaching in a bunch of different subjects, particularly in science. It was noted that, because science is primarily a knowledge based subject (excluding practicals), good explanations, checks for understanding, and combatting misconceptions was, to an AI, as easy as falling off a log. As long as behaviour and expectations were managed, pupils seemed to be doing well. And as an added bonus, staffing costs were actually falling across the country for the first time in years. With large boards in front of entire year groups of 250+, staffing has reduced to little more than 2 or 3 Behaviour Monitors ensuring pupils remain on task. This wasn't much different to what was being offered at some schools in the late 2020's and early 2030's. Back then, teachers on a Microsoft Teams call, broadcast to hundreds of students across the country, would use Microsoft's Study and Learn features to tailor questions to individual students. Now an AI teacher with AI tutors doing pretty much the same but for fractions of the cost. The concept of 25 students in a classroom in 2020 was almost unheard of, now schools of 1000+ can often only have 4 or 5 classes. Microsoft - Study and Learn: AI built for your student Independent - Teachers urge action on class sizes as three-quarters say numbers have gone up In 2030, the DfE commissioned AI organisations to review the national curriculum. The hidden goal was obvious: how could we make it so that the curriculum could be taught by an AI rather than a standard classroom teacher? Was there a way to review a student's essay writing that did not require teacher input? How about the best way to learn a new language? What about listening to them perform a piece of music to then offer them advice on how best to perform Mozart, noticing the literal second at which the student could have done X to be successful? The new national curriculum was released in September 2032. Unions like NASUWT and the NEU complained about it. Their main issue was those involved in their creation. The tech companies. It wasn't a curriculum designed to be delivered by their members, they said. It was designed to be implemented by AI images of colleagues who, since their initial recordings back in 2027, have left the profession. As time went on, many new teachers had this in their school, and saw little issue with it. The strikes stopped and the Overton window shifted. In the run up to its introduction, teachers scrambled to be assessed by tech companies as 'expert teachers' so they could earn a hefty sum to record videos to train their AIs. This was mainly due to the large drop in recruitment of new teachers and many UPS teachers saw the writing on the wall and got out early. Those left remaining saw redundancies and difficulties in obtaining new roles. Schools that went full board with the AIfication of education benefitted massively. Their staffing costs fell rapidly and investments into new, non-AI facilities grew. Art and Design, PE and Drama departments suddenly became state-of-the-art. Academic subjects were now covered with ClassAI, it couldn't replace PE teachers... Schools nowadays do still need staff, mainly to monitor behaviour, maintain the building and commission new contracts. Behaviour Monitors are paid little more than minimum wage now, same with Caretakers. There are rumours the Department for Education and AI Infrastructure (DfEAII) will likely bring contracting in-house, but this is yet to even be piloted. The DfEAII is happy. Every student has their own personalised tutor and access to expert teaching. The treasury is even happier. Back in 2026, 70-85% of a schools budget was staffing, now its a touch above 30%. The investment boom in buildings has slowed as the treasure has sought to claw back spending and tech companies ramping up licencing fees. The Union of School Workers (USW) has been campaigning recently for an increase in funding for AI, but with their numbers now much smaller than when they were formed 10 years ago, they have little say in lobbying politicians for schooling. The AI infrastructure in today's school does require significant investment, but it is still serving its purpose. So what impact is it having on average test scores? Reading age tests in the US began to change in 2025 from longer form content to more short form, easy to understand content. It was argued at the time that this was due to lower attention spans and the lowering of what we could call an adequate reader. But since the introduction of Reading Age Pro Max in England, reading age scores have increased. Coupled with AI, these changes to reading age assessments have seen the Reading Age Pro Max age for English children increase by 6 months on average. Legacy standardized-testing firms are cutting rigor to please students. As for national testing scores, the changes to the GCSEs, renamed back to O Levels in 2038, have not improved much. Independent schools and alternative schools that offer 'real' teachers have seen test score skyrocket, but for the average, run of the mill school, average tests scores have not improved and our ranking in PISA, whilst not decreasing much, has not increased in over a decade. Some argue that we should return to the 'old' style of teaching, where one teacher teaches a small class of 35. It is argued that the relationship building and social elements that used to exist in schools has been eroded in favour of cost saving. Some say this is just typical of the Millennial mentality of a bygone era that never truly existed in the first place. Thanks for reading Joel Kenyon @ Substack!
